Thread title: PEP 830: Add timestamps to exceptions and tracebacks

Opening post by gpshead (author), first sentences:
[p1.s1] This PEP adds an optional timestamp to all exceptions that records when the exception was instantiated with no observable overhead.
[p1.s2] When enabled via environment variable or command-line flag, formatted tracebacks display this timestamp alongside the exception message.
[p1.s3] If you’ve ever debugged a production Python system involving many forms of concurrency and wished you had more information about what happened when, this PEP may be for you.

Known alternatives:
none yet

Posts:
<post n="1" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-12">
[p1.s1] This PEP adds an optional timestamp to all exceptions that records when the exception was instantiated with no observable overhead.
[p1.s2] When enabled via environment variable or command-line flag, formatted tracebacks display this timestamp alongside the exception message.
[p1.s3] If you’ve ever debugged a production Python system involving many forms of concurrency and wished you had more information about what happened when, this PEP may be for you.
[p1.s4] The point at which an exception is logged or rendered with a logging system supplied timestamp is often not the same as the time it happened.
[p1.s5] If you never debug complex applications like that, you won’t even notice that this feature exists.
[p1.s6] It is off by default, to be enabled only by those in environments who feel the above pain.
[p1.s7] Win win.
</post>

<post n="2" author="iritkatriel" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-12">
[p2.s1] I think the time it was raised may be more interesting than the time it was instantiated.
</post>

<post n="3" author="bwoodsend" role="participant" date="2026-04-12">
[p3.s1] Can this not already be done with something like:
[p3.s2] ``` def excepthook(exctype, value, traceback): value.add_note(f"Raised at {datetime.now()}") sys.__excepthook__(exctype, value, traceback) sys.excepthook = excepthook ```
[p3.s3] (P.S.
[p3.s4] It would help if the example in the PEP was self contained so I could try it.)
</post>

<post n="4" author="ncoghlan" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-12" reply_to="2" quotes="2">
[p4.s1] That would be a more intrusive change, though, as the interpreter loop would need to store the info somewhere else until the exception was instantiated when a stateless exception is raised by type.
[p4.s2] User code can also force the two times to match by instantiating when raising (which is necessarily the case for stateful exceptions).
</post>

<post n="5" author="iritkatriel" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-12" reply_to="4" quotes="4">
[p5.s1] I think it can attach the timestamp in `do_raise` (see here) just after the raised type is instantiated.
[p5.s2] I was thinking about cases where the exception is created before the raise.
[p5.s3] Maybe it’s returned from some function, cached, and raised somewhere else at a later time.
[p5.s4] It’s also possible to raise the same exception instance more than once.
[p5.s5] And of course we would need to defined whether the timestamp is overwritten in a reraise (a naked raise or an explicit `raise e’).
[p5.s6] Setting the timestamp at object creation time bypasses these question because the object is only created once.
[p5.s7] But I’m questioning why that is the most semantically meaningful timestamp to use here.
</post>

<post n="6" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-12" reply_to="5">
[p6.s1] How often does code actually have a distinction between time of instantiation and time of raise in practice?
[p6.s2] I understand it is possible to do a bare `raise SomeExceptionType` without an immediately constructing `(”message”)` argument I believe causes this.
[p6.s3] But that one doesn’t matter, `do_raise` immediately calls it to do the instantiation.
[p6.s4] Nevermind that bare raises without `()` don’t feel like a normal idiom I’ve seen in code since basically forever.
[p6.s5] Even in the C API, the `PyErr_Set*` APIs do the same thing from what I can tell by calling `_PyErr_CreateException`.
[p6.s6] It seems like most everything normalizes the exception into an instance pretty quickly.
[p6.s7] Does anyone have practical in-use examples of code creating an exception instance well before the raise, or even the unsatisfiable pattern of (eek!) re-using a pre-created exception instance across many disconnected raises?
[p6.s8] I believe we do this internally for some last-ditch `MemoryError` situations, but that’s a special case that seems fine to ignore.
[p6.s9] It is certainly possible for people to write code in Python or C that does it.
[p6.s10] But why would anyone?
[p6.s11] PEP-830 update TODO: We should probably explicitly zero out any singleton exception instance timestamps we have in our own internals.
[p6.s12] Regardless, while pondering that I’m going to go brush up on the `ceval.h::do_raise` path to better understand possibilities.
</post>

<post n="7" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-12" reply_to="6">
[p7.s1] This is also one of those areas where trying to be perfect could be not worthwhile.
[p7.s2] I expect instantiation time will cover the bulk of use cases.
[p7.s3] If we find otherwise through experience we could change how the time collection is done.
</post>

<post n="8" author="Rosuav" role="participant" date="2026-04-13">
[p8.s1] What are the consequences on internal-use exceptions like `StopIteration`?
[p8.s2] Querying the time of day takes a notable amount of time:
[p8.s3] ``` rosuav@sikorsky:~$ python3 -m timeit -s 'from time import time' 'time()' 10000000 loops, best of 5: 24 nsec per loop rosuav@sikorsky:~$ python3 -m timeit -s 'from time import time' 'for _ in (): pass' 50000000 loops, best of 5: 5.87 nsec per loop rosuav@sikorsky:~$ python3 -m timeit -s 'def time(): pass' 'time()' 20000000 loops, best of 5: 11.7 nsec per loop ```
[p8.s4] and I’d hope that this can be avoided in these situations.
</post>

<post n="9" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="8">
[p9.s1] did you read the PEP? (ie: StopIteration and StopAsyncIteration needs are answered in there already, yes this was worth considering and is a special case!)
</post>

<post n="10" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="6">
[p10.s1] Regarding ceval’s `do_raise` - that probably isn’t the touchpoint to do it if we wanted time of raise rather than instantiation as it is eval loop focused.
[p10.s2] But I think `Python/errors.c::_PyErr_SetRaisedException` might be.
[p10.s3] Assuming everything goes through that rather than diddling with `tstate->current_exception` directly (which feels like a hard assumption to make, though it appears true by my ripgrepping).
</post>

<post n="11" author="dr_carlos" role="participant" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="6" quotes="6">
[p11.s1] I have written code which ‘asserts’ a bunch of things by instantiating a exceptions throughout a function, adding them to a list and then raising them as an `ExceptionGroup` at the end.
[p11.s2] This removes the extra step of raising the exception each time, catching it, only to add it to an exception group.
[p11.s3] I’m not sure if this is best practice or anything, but it’s a pattern that works for me.
[p11.s4] So if the timestamp is added at raise-time, I think this PEP would no longer cover such exceptions as they are never actually raised.
[p11.s5] I’m not sure if this is a good or a bad thing, just something to consider.
</post>

<post n="12" author="Rosuav" role="participant" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="9" quotes="9">
[p12.s1] Doh.
[p12.s2] I did skim it, and I was thinking initially about some others like AttributeError, but then when I went to make the point about the time cost, I switched to StopIteration because it’s easier to demonstrate.
[p12.s3] So, yes, that particular one IS handled (yay!).
[p12.s4] What I should have asked is: will things like `hasattr` calls become slower because of internal time queries?
[p12.s5] ``` rosuav@sikorsky:~$ python3 -m timeit -s 'from time import time' 'time()' 10000000 loops, best of 5: 23.8 nsec per loop rosuav@sikorsky:~$ python3 -m timeit 'hasattr(None, "test")' 20000000 loops, best of 5: 14.4 nsec per loop ```
[p12.s6] Same applies (I think??) to `dict.setdefault` and `__missing__`.
[p12.s7] And maybe I should have stuck with my original thought, since that would have shown me that the time cost isn’t nearly as distinct.
</post>

<post n="13" author="iritkatriel" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="6" quotes="6">
[p13.s1] By ‘bare raise’ I meant a `raise` without args (reraise currently handled exception).
[p13.s2] I’m not concerned about the case of raising a type, it gets instantiated almost immediately so I don’t see a difference.
</post>

<post n="14" author="AndersMunch" role="participant" date="2026-04-13">
[p14.s1] About this:
[p14.s2] A Python API to toggle timestamps at runtime is unnecessary complexity.
[p14.s3] Applications that want timestamps are expected to enable them in their environment; a runtime toggle would make it harder to reason about program state.
[p14.s4] Could we please not add features to Python that are managed from outside of Python, and can only be managed from outside of Python, unless the nature of the feature necessitates it?
[p14.s5] I want to program in Python, not in shell script.
</post>

<post n="15" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="13" quotes="13">
[p15.s1] The currently handled exception already has a timestamp and the original place it was raised from is the correct place for the time to have been recorded.
</post>

<post n="16" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="5" quotes="5">
[p16.s1] Okay so I gather this is what you were talking about in regards to the bare `raise` that reraises the currently being handled exception as one example.
[p16.s2] I do not think it is solvable to store a timestamp at every point a raise happens (complex and generally not necessary).
[p16.s3] It either needs to be time of instantiation, or time of first raise.
[p16.s4] Time of most recent raise could be far removed from the appropriate spot even in perfectly linear chains of exception handlers doing a reraise after running additional logic.
[p16.s5] It’s an interesting thought to record each of the re-raises along the way, but no longer trivial.
</post>

<post n="15" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="13" quotes="13">
[p15.s1] The currently handled exception already has a timestamp and the original place it was raised from is the correct place for the time to have been recorded.

<post n="16" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-13" reply_to="5" quotes="5">
[p16.s1] Okay so I gather this is what you were talking about in regards to the bare `raise` that reraises the currently being handled exception as one example.

<post n="17" author="vstinner" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-13">
[p17.s1] I think that this idea (adding a timestamp to exceptions) was already discussed previously, but I failed to find the link.
[p17.s2] Or maybe it was your PR gh-129337 that you created in January 2025.
[p17.s3] I found the recent project dttb (created last January) which uses `sys.excepthook` to add a timestamp to exceptions.
[p17.s4] It uses `datetime.datetime.now()` and so has a resolution of 1 microsecond.
[p17.s5] It formats the timestamp at the beginning:
[p17.s6] ``` [2026-01-28 14:30:15.123456+08:00] Traceback (most recent call last): ... Error: something wrong ```
[p17.s7] I find it interesting to put the timestamp at the start and don’t change `str(exc)`.
[p17.s8] Specification:
[p17.s9] A new read/write attribute `__timestamp_ns__` is added to `BaseException`.
[p17.s10] It stores nanoseconds since the Unix epoch
[p17.s11] You should mention that’s a timestamp in the UTC time zone.
[p17.s12] When timestamps are disabled, or for control flow exceptions (see below), the value is `0`.
[p17.s13] You should also use the value `0` when reading the clock fails.
[p17.s14] It’s rare but it can happen when the syscall is blocked by a sandbox (by mistake).
[p17.s15] For the Python API (`exc.__timestamp_ns__` attribute), would it make sense to return `None` instead of `0` when the timestamp is not set?
[p17.s16] `PYTHON_TRACEBACK_TIMESTAMPS` environment variable Set to `us` or `1` for microsecond-precision decimal timestamps, `ns` for nanoseconds, or `iso` for ISO 8601 UTC format.
[p17.s17] Empty, unset, or `0` disables timestamps (the default).
[p17.s18] Can you mention that ISO 8601 format has a resolution of 1 microsecond?
[p17.s19] Display Format:
[p17.s20] The `us` format produces `<@1776017164.530916>` and the `ns` format produces `<@1776017178687320256ns>`.
[p17.s21] I would prefer to use `<@1776017178.687320256>` format for `ns`, similar to the `us` format but with 3 extra digits after the dot.
[p17.s22] For example, using this format you can copy/paste the number to `datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp()` and `time.gmtime()`:
[p17.s23] ``` >>> import datetime as dt >>> print(dt.datetime.fromtimestamp(1776017178.687320256)) 2026-04-12 20:06:18.687320 >>> import time >>> time.gmtime(1776017178.687320256) time.struct_time(tm_year=2026, tm_mon=4, tm_mday=12, tm_hour=18, tm_min=6, tm_sec=18, tm_wday=6, tm_yday=102, tm_isdst=0) ```
[p17.s24] Performance Measurements.
[p17.s25] FYI Linux and other operating systems provide a `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` clock faster than `CLOCK_REALTIME` but with a worse resolution.
[p17.s26] For example, on Linux 6.19.10 with glibc 2.42, I measured in Python that `CLOCK_REALTIME` has a resolution of 137 nanoseconds, whereas `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` only has a resolution of 1 ms!
[p17.s27] I don’t think that 1 ms resolution is enough for exception timestamps.
[p17.s28] Reading `CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE` takes `28.8 ns +- 0.7 ns`, whereas reading `CLOCK_REALTIME` takes `40.7 ns +- 1.6 ns`.
[p17.s29] `TracebackException` and the public formatting functions (`print_exc`, `print_exception`, `format_exception`, `format_exception_only`) gain a `no_timestamp` keyword argument (default `False`) that suppresses timestamp display even when globally enabled.
[p17.s30] I dislike double negation (ex: `no_timestamp=False`).
[p17.s31] Would it be possible to change the parameter to `timestamp` instead (ex: `timestamp=True`)?
[p17.s32] Rejected Ideas: Millisecond Precision.
[p17.s33] Why not also offering the choice to format a timestamp with microsecond resolution?
[p17.s34] (`PYTHON_TRACEBACK_TIMESTAMPS=ms`)
</post>

<post n="18" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-14" reply_to="17">
[p18.s1] The draft PR has been around a while as i’ve been noodling on doing it since early 2025.
[p18.s2] I presented the idea to the room in our Cambridge Core Team Sprint last September.
[p18.s3] The feedback there led me to tweaking the behavior a bit (to not collect the times at all when the feature is disabled rather than just controlling their display), better documenting the what and why, and turning it into a PEP.
</post>

<post n="19" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-14" reply_to="17" quotes="17">
[p19.s1] Using the `sys.excepthook` singleton does not work for this purpose.
[p19.s2] It does not get called at the time of raise or construction, which would defeat the purpose for this use case of having every exception raised in an ExceptionGroup carry a timestamp at the point it occurred.
[p19.s3] It is also global state that other things can (and do) clobber for their own purposes.
[p19.s4] FWIW, that `dttb` library was advertised in a drive by spammy comment on my github tracking issue for this feature a month ago. (unclear if that was by the author or by their AI bot) Regardless it is not an equivalent.
[p19.s5] A feeling that it already offers plenty of choices?
[p19.s6] Supporting this would also be easy and suggests your idea to format the `ns` value as a decimal has merit as `ms` `us` and `ns` would all be formatted the same that way.
[p19.s7] Easy to add, but I don’t think it’d be necessary.
[p19.s8] If anything I could see dropping `us` support and only offering `ns` and `iso` modes (though probably using your decimal format for `ns`).
[p19.s9] For the same reason, I do not want to support custom timestamp formatting strings other than `iso`.
[p19.s10] It just adds complexity for no meaningful value.
[p19.s11] I thought that was implied by being seconds since the unix epoch like everything in POSIX time land.
[p19.s12] I’ll add the note to make it clear in my next PEP update.
</post>

<post n="20" author="gpshead" role="author" date="2026-04-14" reply_to="19" quotes="17">
[p20.s1] re: Timer resolution - we always collect a nanosecond resolution value (which most OSes provide) regardless of the display format using `PyTime_TimeRaw`.
[p20.s2] Thus the attr being named `__timestamp_ns__` See cpython/Objects/exceptions.c at 2672099c67cbeeb03c0dcba55e7975c999887d74 · python/cpython · GitHub
[p20.s3] So do I. Now I need to remember why I did that… I think it came from the only reason to ever use the new kwarg at all being to disable the display.
[p20.s4] But that’s still better as `timestamp=False`.
[p20.s5] BUT a `timestamp=True` default or someone oddly explicitly passing that could be incorrectly interpreted as always displaying one even if collection is not enabled (not possible or it’d be 0) and no need for this to be a tri-state.
[p20.s6] Which could lead to wordier but accurate API name such as `allow_timestamps=False` with a default of `True`.
[p20.s7] A bit of a bikeshed.
</post>

<post n="21" author="ncoghlan" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-14" reply_to="7" quotes="7">
[p21.s1] Recording “time of first raise” timestamps as a “Deferred, but not rejected” idea sounds good to me.
[p21.s2] It might be possible, but it’s not obviously easy, and it’s far from clear that it’s necessary, so including it in the initial iteration carries a high risk of introducing significant complexity for negligible benefit.
</post>

<post n="22" author="iritkatriel" role="maintainer" date="2026-04-15">
[p22.s1] We can do this with monitoring:

[p29.s1] The SC has discussed and while we are generally positive about PEP 830 - Add timestamps to exceptions and tracebacks, we have decided to defer making a decision on this PEP until Python 3.16.
[p29.s2] We have feedback on collection and on the opt-in/display story that we’d like to see worked through before we make a decision.
[p29.s3] On the collection:
[p29.s4] - The current performance numbers do not cover Windows or shared-library configurations (which may see significantly more overhead). We’d like to see numbers for those environments incorporated into the PEP so we can better evaluate the overhead claim across platforms.
[p29.s5] - Pickle output depends on the timestamp collection state, which we find awkward. We’d prefer an opt-out, either by not collecting, or by not pickling the timestamp attribute even when collection is enabled.
[p29.s6] On opt-in and display:
[p29.s7] - The PEP appeals to CPython convention to justify silent-ignore on invalid env var values, but that convention is really for boolean toggles (e.g. `PYTHONFAULTHANDLER`, `PYTHONDEVMODE`) and not for enum-shaped flags (e.g. `PYTHON_GIL`, `PYTHON_FROZEN_MODULES`, `PYTHONTRACEMALLOC`, `PYTHON_CPU_COUNT`, `PYTHONHASHSEED`). Enum-shaped flags by and large fail-fatal on invalid values, and `PYTHON_TRACEBACK_TIMESTAMPS` should follow the convention of that peer group. This behavior should also be aligned across the env var and `-X` paths to avoid a confusing user experience and bifurcation of documentation.
[p29.s8] - `PYTHON_TRACEBACK_TIMESTAMPS` and `-X traceback_timestamps=` should accept one value per meaning. Each precision option should have a single canonical string (e.g. `ns`, `us`, `ms`, `iso`), with an explicit `off` for disabled. Equivalents like `empty`, `0`, and `1` should be rejected as invalid rather than silently aliased to one of the canonical values.
[p29.s9] - The current proposed timestamp suffix appears on the message line in formatted traceback output and is per-occurrence, which means tooling that captures stderr or formatted tracebacks and matches on the message line sees a different string for every exception instance. The discussion thread raised header-line placement as an alternative that avoids this. We don’t think message-line placement is necessarily wrong, but the PEP should further justify the choice with a clear rationale and close out the open issue regarding display location. Further, placing the timestamp at the end of the line obscures it in ways that can be difficult to see.
[p29.s10] - Opt-out for doctest printing will likely break code and is backward incompatible. This is because doctests can be very sensitive to display output. We’d prefer an opt-in flag, e.g. `doctest.INCLUDE_EXCEPTION_TIMESTAMPS` which are not enabled by default.
[p29.s11] - Similarly `test.support.force_no_traceback_timestamps` should probably be enabled by default, possibly with a differently named flag to enable traceback timestamps in the stdlib test suite.
[p29.s12] Thanks again for your work on this PEP, we look forward to discussing again with revisions.
</post>

[p3.s1] - Sampling profilers like this require a extremelly tight coupling with CPython internals. They depend on accessing low-level execution state with minimal overhead, supporting multi-threaded programs, free-threading, async code, and even remote attachment. All of this requires syncing the profilers AND the features, even between patch versions. Because of this deep integration, changes in CPython internals can easily break or degrade sampling profilers (this happens constantly and is very painful for everyone). Keeping it in the stdlib ensures synchronization with those changes.
[p3.s2] - Having the profiler in the stdlib ensures users have a high performance profiler with these features working on the release of CPython and they don’t need to wait months or years until the other tools reverse engineer all the ways CPython broke them or make their life harder.
[p3.s3] - We can use the profiler to profile Python code during development of CPython. Normally not having into the sodlib means no profiler works until the release so we cannot benefit from it during development cycles.
[p3.s4] - The stdlib now lacks a performant profiler that works for the different things that we offer (free threading, asyncio, …etc). Including a well-supported, zero-overhead profiler in the stdlib provides a known baseline and reference implementation that other tools can use as a baseline or emulate. It also avoids fragmentation, which is especially important in performance tooling. The PEP goes into some more detail.
[p3.s5] - It also provides a stable, officially supported reference implementation that external tools can study or build on without needing to resort to undocumented or fragile techniques. This will help everyone know a baseline on how to adapt their things to new versions and don’t force them to have to find out contorted ways to keep the use case working and ensures that we don’t break these tools on every release.
[p3.s6] - Including this in the stdlib helps steer users away from outdated tools like `profile`, and toward modern, efficient practices.
[p3.s7] I don’t mind that If everyone else agrees.

[p3.s9] One downside of this is that `profiling` exists on PyPI but `profilers` doesn’t.

<post n="1" author="Zac-HD" role="author" date="2025-05-22">
[p1.s1] TL;DR: Let’s allow `async with` to accept both sync and async context managers in a single statement, as long as there’s at least one async context manager present.
[p1.s2] This would eliminate the nested indentation that currently plagues mixed context manager code.
[p1.s3] GitHub issue here.
[p1.s4] ## The Problem
[p1.s5] If you write async Python with context managers, you’ve hit this pain point: every time you need to mix sync and async context managers, you get punished with another level of indentation:
[p1.s6] ``` # status quo: the staircase of doom async with acquire_lock() as lock: with open('config.json') as f: async with connect_to_db() as db: with temp_directory() as tmpdir: # Your actual code is now 16 spaces deep; # you and your colleagues are sad. ```
[p1.s7] You can get around this with `contextlib.AsyncExitStack()`, but only at the cost of some serious footguns for the unwary (e.g. mis-nesting contexts, the sharp edges in `.pop_all()`, etc).
[p1.s8] ## The Proposal
[p1.s9] Allow `async with` to accept both sync and async context managers:
[p1.s10] ``` async with ( acquire_lock() as lock, open('config.json') as f, connect_to_db() as db, temp_directory() as tmpdir, ): # Your code starts at a reasonable indentation # Your colleagues might actually review your PR ```
[p1.s11] The rule is simple: if there’s at least one async context manager in the group, you can use `async with` for the whole thing.
[p1.s12] This is semantically identical to a safe use of `AsyncExitStack`, but much prettier code and harder to get wrong.
[p1.s13] ## Unsatisfying workarounds
[p1.s14] #### Add checkpoints
[p1.s15] Wrapping sync context managers in async helpers adds await points where your async framework can switch tasks.
[p1.s16] Context manager boundaries are terrible places for task switches - they often handle timeouts, locks, or error recovery - and so this can introduce bugs, as well as the performance overhead.
[p1.s17] ``` def as_acm(ctx): @asynccontextmanager def inner(): with ctx as val: await sleep(0) yield val return inner() async with ( acquire_lock() as lock, as_acm(open('config.json')) as f, connect_to_db() as db, as_acm(temp_directory()) as tmpdir, ): # hope you didn't need an atomic section there... ```
[p1.s18] #### An `AsyncExitStack` helper function
[p1.s19] The semantics of a `async with multicontext(...)` helper are better than the `as_acm()` trick, but you lose the locality of `as` clauses, and with that the code becomes uglier and harder to understand:
[p1.s20] ``` @asynccontextmanager async def multicontext(*cms): assert any(hasattr(cm, "__aenter__") for cm in cms) async with AsyncExitStack() as stack: enter, aenter = stack.enter_context, stack.enter_async_context yield tuple( (enter(cm) if hasattr(cm, "__enter__") else await aenter(cm)) for cm in cms ) async with ( acquire_lock(), open('config.json'), connect_to_db(), temp_directory(), ) as (lock, db, f, tmpdir): # Wait, which order were those in again? ```
[p1.s21] ## Implementation Considerations
[p1.s22] The change should be straightforward:
[p1.s23] - Runtime check that at least one async context manager is present
[p1.s24] - Proper handling of `__enter__`/`__exit__` vs `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`
[p1.s25] The semantics are clear: sync context managers use their normal protocol, async ones use the async protocol, execution order remains left-to-right.
[p1.s26] `AsyncExitStack` already does this; I’m just proposing to support it directly at the statement level where code can be as clean and simple as possible.
[p1.s27] ## Prior Art
[p1.s28] I’ve been using both of the “unsatisfying workarounds” above in production Trio code; they do indeed work and are indeed unsatisfying.
[p1.s29] We would be delighted to switch over to using the `async with` statement as soon as possible.
[p1.s30] ## Backwards Compatibility
[p1.s31] This is purely additive.
[p1.s32] All existing code continues to work.
[p1.s33] The only “breaking” change is that code that was previously a `RuntimeError` would now work, with the only reasonable non-error semantics.
[p1.s34] ## What do you think?
[p1.s35] Am I missing some crucial consideration here?
[p1.s36] Is there a technical blocker I’m not seeing?
[p1.s37] For those using structured concurrency with `asyncio.TaskGroup` or Trio or AnyIO, this would be particularly nice - you could finally group your timeout/cancellation contexts naturally with your resource contexts without the indentation penalty.
</post>

[p14.s2] There’s the practical reason that the interpreter doesn’t have a reliable way to know how to execute a checkpoint - that’s a callback into your currently-active async framework of choice, and there are several that could even be active simultaneously in a single thread.

[p16.s1] Hi all - after some earlier discussion, I’m pleased to present PEP 806 for discussion.
[p16.s2] It’s in most ways a very small proposal, which would make a surprisingly large difference for my code!
[p16.s3] Feedback, questions, requests for clarification, etc. all most welcome.
[p16.s4] ## Abstract
[p16.s5] Python allows the `with` and `async with` statements to handle multiple context managers in a single statement, so long as they are all respectively synchronous or asynchronous.
[p16.s6] When mixing synchronous and asynchronous context managers, developers must use deeply nested statements or use risky workarounds such as overuse of `AsyncExitStack`.
[p16.s7] We therefore propose to allow `with` statements to accept both synchronous and asynchronous context managers in a single statement by prefixing individual async context managers with the `async` keyword.
[p16.s8] This change eliminates unnecessary nesting, improves code readability, and improves ergonomics without making async code any less explicit.
[p16.s9] For example:
[p16.s10] ``` async def process_data(): async with acquire_lock() as lock: with temp_directory() as tmpdir: async with connect_to_db(cache=tmpdir) as db: with open('config.json', encoding='utf-8') as f: # We're now 16 spaces deep before any actual logic config = json.load(f) await db.execute(config['query']) # ... more processing ```

[p16.s12] ``` async def process_data(): with ( async acquire_lock() as lock, temp_directory() as tmpdir, async connect_to_db(cache=tmpdir) as db, open('config.json', encoding='utf-8') as f, ): config = json.load(f) await db.execute(config['query']) # ... more processing ```

[p23.s2] One of the best design decisions with async/await was making asynchronous code unmistakably distinct: when you see `async with`, you immediately know “this can suspend execution.”
[p23.s3] The proposal blurs this by allowing `with async ctx()` which looks like a sync statement with an async detail buried inside.
[p23.s4] At a glance, you lose the clear signal that this block involves async operations.
[p23.s5] The current forced nesting actually serves a purpose: it makes you think about the async/sync boundary and makes it visually obvious which scopes are async.
[p23.s6] The motivating example showing “16 spaces deep” is already a code smell that should be refactored regardless of async: you shouldn’t have four nested context managers in the first place.
[p23.s7] If deep nesting is genuinely necessary, the explicitness of separate `async with` blocks is worth the verbosity because it maintains clarity about where suspension points exist.
[p23.s8] In my view the ergonomic improvement isn’t worth compromising the visual distinction that makes async code safe and maintainable.

[p27.s1] On behalf of the Python Steering Council: We’ve chosen to reject PEP 806, “Mixed sync/async context managers with precise async marking”.
[p27.s2] We thank Zac for the careful survey and write-up, and we acknowledge that the nesting pattern the PEP describes is a real annoyance for code that mixes sync and async context managers.
[p27.s3] However, the cost of adding new syntax to Python is very high: a permanent addition to the grammar is paid for by every parser, AST consumer, linter, formatter, type checker, and teaching resource in the ecosystem, and it is carried forward by every Python programmer from here on.
[p27.s4] The problem this PEP addresses, while genuine, does not in our view meet that bar.
[p27.s5] The PEP’s own survey suggests adoption would be limited to a specific subset of async code that also uses synchronous context managers, and that narrow payoff is not enough on its own to justify new syntax.
[p27.s6] In addition to that background concern, we have several more specific reservations:
[p27.s7] - The proposal introduces two valid spellings with different rules. Under this PEP, async with ctx(): and with async ctx(): would both be valid spellings of an async context manager entry, with different compositional rules: the former disallows mixing, the latter permits it. The PEP explicitly defers style enforcement to linters and formatters, but we are reluctant to ship syntax whose usability depends on external tooling to decide which of two legal forms is idiomatic.
[p27.s8] - We have some concerns about how with async interacts with the existing async marking convention. Today every line performing asynchronous work begins with async or await as its first non-whitespace token, which is a property readers and static analysis tools often rely on. Placing async as an item-level prefix inside a parenthesised with block changes that, and the PEP’s own recommendation to keep async with for single-line statements suggests the authors share some of this concern. On balance we would prefer to preserve the existing convention rather than loosen it for a syntactic convenience.
[p27.s9] - Existing workarounds are adequate for the cases the PEP addresses. contextlib.AsyncExitStack and the as_acm() helper pattern already cover the mixed sync/async case. The PEP’s objection to as_acm() rests on the await sleep(0) cancellation checkpoint breaking the property that syntactic await/async for/async with always yields to the scheduler, but the PEP itself acknowledges that few codebases enforce this property today. We would be receptive to a proposal for a stdlib version of as_acm(), with or without the checkpoint, as a smaller and more targeted change.
[p27.s10] None of this is to dismiss the underlying pain point.
[p27.s11] We would encourage interested parties to continue exploring library-level solutions, and we think the survey data gathered for this PEP would be valuable input into such a discussion.
[p27.s12] Thanks to Zac for the work, and to everyone who contributed to the discussion.
</post>

[p1.s5] That is currently a blocker for https://github.com/apache/airflow/issues/37785
[p1.s6] Why `--user` flag is useful and why we use it in Airflow?
[p1.s7] Using `--user` flag is pretty useful when you want to have an optimized image - because such `.local` folders can be copied between different stage of the image (based on the same base image and prod libraries installed) and you can copy the whole `.local` folder between the stages after packages are installed - which means that the final stage of the image does not have to have `build-essentials`/ compilers installed.
[p1.s8] You could do the same with `venv` if you keep it in the same folder, but that looses an essential capability of creating venv dynamically containing all the packages you have in your `.local` folder.
[p1.s9] When you have your `--user` installed packages, and you create a new venv with `--system-site-packages`, the packages installed in `.local` folder are also installed in the new venv.
[p1.s10] This does not work when you create a new `venv` from another `venv` because `--system-site-packages` are only the ones installed in the system.
[p1.s11] While I can think of some creative ways (maybe I will find some) - having an equivalent of `--user` installation by `uv pip install` would be a great simplification for our case to support the users who want to use `uv` (and seems that there is already a need for that looking at the https://github.com/apache/airflow/issues/37785
</post>

<post n="8" author="potiuk" role="author" date="2024-02-29">
[p8.s1] Yes.
[p8.s2] In Airflow we have something called `PythonVirtualenvOperator`.
[p8.s3] Airflow has operators (4000+ of them 😱 ) that can do tasks related to some "stuff" to do - some of them are specific ("GoogleCloudJobOperator`, `ApacheSparkJobOperator`, `CreateEKSClusterOperator`) but we have a number of a few generic ones `BashOperator`, `PythonOperator`, `ExternalPythonOperator` - runs python code on prepared virtualenv.
[p8.s4] All of those are unaffected, but PythonVirtualenvOperator is special - because what it does is:
[p8.s5] It creates a new virtualenv based on requirements, python version.
[p8.s6] One of the options (only valid if your python version matches the `system` version) is `system-site-packages` - when True, the new venv will have `airflow` and all airflow packages pre-installed.
[p8.s7] This is super important, because we serialize arguments that we pass to the operator, and de-serialze return value from it, as interface between airflow and the "new venv" method executed.
[p8.s8] And in order to serialize some objects, the target venv should have the "airflow + often other packages" installed.
[p8.s9] Moreover the python code to be executed (basically a methpd) can do some local imports - expecting airflow or other packages to be installed.
[p8.s10] The `--system-site-packages` in this case is best, because you do not have to explicitly specify which airflow version or which other packages you have to have installed.
[p8.s11] You can specify `extra` dependencies to add - but having the `base same as the Airflow execution environment` is often necessary.
[p8.s12] Here howto: https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/howto/operator/python.html#pythonvirtualenvoperator Here Python API: https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/_api/airflow/operators/python/index.html#airflow.operators.python.PythonVirtualenvOperator
</post>

<post n="9" author="potiuk" role="author" date="2024-02-29">
[p9.s1] Under the hood, the operator does:
[p9.s2] ``` def _generate_virtualenv_cmd(tmp_dir: str, python_bin: str, system_site_packages: bool) -> list[str]: cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "virtualenv", tmp_dir] if system_site_packages: cmd.append("--system-site-packages") if python_bin is not None: cmd.append(f"--python={python_bin}") return cmd ```
</post>

[p13.s3] > The starting point I have is this:
[p13.s4] using the `--system-site-packages` while creating the virtual environment should make this error message gone.
[p13.s5] If we take a step back, `--user` wouldn't be quite useful in this case since there's already an virtualenv.
[p13.s6] > And I think there were lots of related discussions.
[p13.s7] Here is one: https://github.com/pypa/pip/issues/6375
[p13.s8] I skimmed through it, and it looks like the issue was mainly about `--editable` install breaking when there's `pyproject.toml` file.
[p13.s9] It doesn't seem like `--user` flag had anything to do with it, since, according to the original issue: `both pip install --user -e . and pip install -e . fail`.
[p13.s10] From what I understand, PEP 517 itself discusses allowing projects to specify different build systems through `pyproject.toml`.
[p13.s11] The build process should be independent from where the packages are installed.
[p13.s12] Not sure how that would impact user site installation.
[p13.s13] > Personally I consider --user feature of pip as should be depreacated ... there were some discussions on deprecating it,
[p13.s14] `--user` was introduced over a decade ago in PEP 370.
[p13.s15] I also saw [this thread about deprecating it](https://groups.google.com/g/dev-python/c/jeb-tiiiRcE/m/JTe6EHGHDQAJ). some replies were not in favor of deprecation, for example:
[p13.s16] ``` Given that we're working towards making user site-packages the default install location in pip, removing that feature at the interpreter level would be rather counterproductive :) Virtual environments are a useful tool if you're a professional developer, but for a lot of folks just doing ad hoc personal scripting, they're more complexity than is needed, and the simple "my packages" vs "the system's package" split is a better option. (It's also rather useful for bootstrapping tools like "pipsi" - "pip install --user pipsi", then "pipsi install" the other commands you want access to). Cheers, Nick. ```
[p13.s17] If we do a quick search on GitHub for the `--user` flag: https://github.com/search?q=%22pip+install+--user%22&type=code&p=1 we'll see it's still widely used
[p13.s18] Though I haven't used `--user` much lately, thanks to `venv` and Docker containers, it's still a popular choice for many Python users for installing packages without needing admin privileges in many environments other than CI
[p13.s19] ---
[p13.s20] Putting `--user` flag in `uv` would bring some of the complexity accumulated in `pip` over the years.
[p13.s21] PR #2352 was my preliminary attempt to fit it into the `uv pip` implementation without introducing too much complexity as the [script](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/main/crates/uv-interpreter/src/get_interpreter_info.py) does the heavy lifting here.
[p13.s22] I haven't looked into every combination of how `--user` flag would play with other `pip` flags, but it would take some effort to make it compatible with the behavior of `pip` for sure.
[p13.s23] Ultimately, it's up to the uv team to decide whether to support it.

[p16.s12] You get an error telling you tha tno `virtualenv` is detected and possibly that you can use `--python` to point to a python installation.

[p46.s3] I was in the same camp "venv in container images is a bloat" - and this was for me the main reason why I opened the issue, but since then I found out that when I create venv in `~./.local` - and simply set `VIRTUAL_ENV` vatiable to point to it and having `~/.local/bin` on the PATH as first entry does precisely what everyone needs here:
[p46.s4] * no need to explain user to do `activate`
[p46.s5] * `activate` merely sets the `VIRTUAL_ENV` variable and inserts PATH entry - and this is as specified in venv defintion, so you can do precisely the same in your container image or environment definition
[p46.s6] * it also nicely retains packages installed in `.local` when you create a new virtual environment with `--system` flag (which was the reason why I opened the issue) - which means that you can nicely create and activate new venvs from such `.local` venv
[p46.s7] * this all adds virtually no overhead comparing to `--user` flag
[p46.s8] I believe now that there is no particular reason to have `--user` flag, really.
[p46.s9] People who say that they do not want to maintain extra scripts are really talking about running two commands.
[p46.s10] People mentioned in the discussion thread here, that they do not want to teach their users about venv, and the approach above 100% solves that.
[p46.s11] You don't have to.
[p46.s12] You just create the venv and set the right environments for them and they can continue using `uv pip install` or `pip install` and it will **just work**.
[p46.s13] Mission accomplished.

[p91.s7] `--user` was that thing, but that's fine, we'll have to find some other method - such as `conda` or using a Python where the `pip` can install into the system without complaint.
[p91.s8] I'm happy to explain why the assumptions are not correct for beginners, but I don't want to extend this thread for those who aren't working with beginners.
</post>

[p92.s1] A note: it’s not just a flag from pip, it’s the concept of user packages specified in PEP 370 and compatible with multiple tools.
[p92.s2] One example: on debian and derivatives, bash includes ~/.local/bin in PATH by default if it exists.
[p92.s3] So pip install --user sometool is a valid and easy way to be able to run sometool without more docs or setup.

<post n="93" author="potiuk" role="author" date="2025-02-18">
[p93.s1] > I'm happy to explain why the assumptions are not correct for beginners, but I don't want to extend this thread for those who aren't working with beginners.
[p93.s2] But the thing is that `uv tool` does exactly that service to beginners.
[p93.s3] It installs the tool you want in it's own virtualenv but it does not even tell the user where it is or that it does it.
[p93.s4] It can't be any easier than that.
[p93.s5] Also if you want to develop something with python you do:

[p93.s7] * `uv add dependency`
[p93.s8] * `uv run whatever`
[p93.s9] As a beginner, you don't even have to have python installed, `uv` will download and install binary version of python from `python-standalone` project that is installed in less than few seconds.
[p93.s10] All the "pesky details" of setting up python and venv are completely hidden from you, and you don't even have to be aware it's there.
[p93.s11] Again - it can't get any simpler than that.
[p93.s12] So maybe your comments apply to the ways how beginners **used** to have problems with starting with Python before `uv`.
[p93.s13] Simply `uv` proposes different - way simpler - workflows for beginners, that utilise `venv` under the hood.
[p93.s14] I'd argue that even telling the beginner they should use `--user` is way more complex than the worfklows that `uv` proposes.
[p93.s15] > A note: it’s not just a flag from pip, it’s the concept of user packages specified in PEP 370 and compatible with multiple tools.
[p93.s16] One example: on debian and derivatives, bash includes ~/.local/bin in PATH by default if it exists.
[p93.s17] So pip install --user sometool is a valid and easy way to be able to run sometool without more docs or setup.
[p93.s18] And yes, I am (painfully) aware of PEP 370 and I am aware how universally problematic it turned out to be for `packaging` maintainers.
[p93.s19] And I eventually - after initial concerns, and having experienced a lot of problems with `--user` in the past, think that the idea of proposing a different, way more maintainable and less problematic solution (and not supporting --user) is a very sound one.
</post>

[p95.s4] By "beginner" I mean someone who is expecting to start an interactive Python console of some sort and do something like `import pygame` or `import pandas`.
[p95.s5] Running some Python command line tool is not a very common beginner task.
[p95.s6] > Also if you want to develop something with python you do: > > * `uv init` > > * `uv add dependency` > > * `uv run whatever` > > > As a beginner, you don't even have to have python installed, `uv` will download and install binary version of python from `python-standalone` project that is installed in less than few seconds.

[p95.s8] Well - yes it can.
[p95.s9] Because a) that won't match nearly all tutorials out there, and b) it depends on the user keeping in mind that they need to stay in the same directory (or subdirectory thereof) to get the relevant virtualenv.
[p95.s10] So if they, for example, do `cd ..` then they've lost their packages, for reasons that won't be obvious to them.
[p95.s11] Just for reference, in a course we taught in Berkeley, to stats students, we had to include a class on the filesystem in the terminal, because many inexperienced computer users have a hazy idea of how files are arranged on the computer, beyond the idea of a "Folder".
[p95.s12] I find that many developers haven't come across these kind of problems, and indeed they are easy to miss if you don't have quite close contact with early learners.
</post>
